changes.after: A person shares something that explains what they want: a prototype, a document or plain words. This feature reads it and drafts one business intent for each need the product meets for its user. A business intent names that need in its users' words, and holds an outcome, why the business wants it, who asks for it, a proof someone can measure and any limits. The person then confirms or drops each one. Each confirmed intent is saved as a page in the product model, linked to the Sources it came from.

changes.after: This feature finds each domain the product sits in and writes a full page for it. A domain is a field the industry names, such as customer relationship management or e-commerce. The feature asks two questions in order: which field does the product serve, and which job does it do there? Each answer can be a domain, so a product often sits in more than one. It works from business intents, a typed goal, a prototype's capture or any mix of them. With none of those, it asks for a goal.
changes.add: The model needs domains because they group its capabilities into fields the industry knows, at the level a business leader talks about.

changes.old: - A knowledge shelf comes first. A domain with no shelf gets a proposal that names it as its research names it, with the research links. The name never comes from the product's screens or sample data. The run records the proposal and goes on.
changes.new: - A knowledge shelf comes first. A domain with no shelf gets a proposal that names it as its research names it, with the research links. The name never comes from the product's screens or sample data. The reason: a domain is a field the industry names, and sample data is only an example of what the product handles. The run records the proposal and goes on.

changes.old: - From a capture, every main section must sit in a domain, with the line from the shelf or research that covers its work and where that line is from. For a section no field covers, the run researches the field that does that work and never stretches a found field over it.
changes.new: - From a capture, every main section must sit in a domain, with the line from the shelf or research that covers its work and where that line is from. A main section is a main part of the prototype, such as a tab, a top menu item or a part of its first screen. For a section no field covers, the run researches the field that does that work and never stretches a found field over it. The grounding check is a script that tests this. It checks that each domain has its shelf or research and its Sources, and that each main section sits in a domain.

changes.old: - A page that exists is grown. A light page is raised to a full one and keeps what it said. An entry's depth never goes down, no domain is added twice, and a run with nothing new changes nothing.
changes.new: - A page that exists is grown. A light page is raised to a full one and keeps what it said. The reason: no one play owns a domain page, so each play writes what it knows and a later play raises it. An entry's depth never goes down, no domain is added twice, and a run with nothing new changes nothing.

changes.old: - The profile stays rough, at the directional state. The run never sets it firm, because the capabilities' real needs are not known yet.
changes.new: - The profile stays rough, at the directional state. Directional means the profile holds only the product's shape and rough quality levels. The run never sets it firm, because the capabilities' real needs are not known yet.

changes.old: - One checkpoint shows each domain and the profile, with the real changes to the model. A learned policy may pass a known shape of change with no wait, but only when no check found a blocking problem. Each crossing goes in a log. A cancel puts the model back.
changes.new: - One checkpoint shows each domain and the profile, with the real changes to the model. Run by hand, a checkpoint is where the run stops and waits for the person's yes. The reason for one: the person reviews the whole change once, and nothing is committed before that. A learned policy may pass a known shape of change with no wait, but only when no check found a blocking problem. A learned policy is a project rule learned from the person's earlier answers. A shape of change the person approved three times in a row, with no edit, may then pass. The reason: the person has already approved that shape. Each crossing goes in a log. A cancel puts the model back.

changes.old: This feature writes a full page for each capability, creates the capability's features with their pages, and sets what the capability needs in quality and compliance. It takes its work from three places: the capabilities a person names, every capability in the model still at the directional depth, and the capabilities a prototype's screens show. changes.new: This feature writes a full page for each capability, creates the capability's features with their pages, and sets what the capability needs in quality and compliance. It takes its work from three places: the capabilities a person names, every capability in the model still at the directional depth, and the capabilities a prototype's screens show. A capability at the directional depth has a short page with only its directional intent. This feature raises it to full depth, called detailed in the model's index, with its benefit hypothesis, boundary, guiding rules and features. One run does all of them together. It is the last detailing step, so the writing is complete but still in product words, not code. The earlier steps are Specify intents and Specify domains, which write the business intents and the domains, but it needs neither to run first.

changes.new: Status: built, except checking each ICE against the rubric. An ICE is the agent's intent for one capability or feature: what an agent must make true there, for whom, and how it is checked. The rubric is the written rule for what a good ICE looks like.

changes.old: - In: the capability's knowledge shelf, and the product profile as it stands when the run starts.

changes.old: - A capability seeded here holds only what its source said: the person's recorded answers, or the screens it was read from. The save refuses any other seed.
changes.new: - A capability seeded here holds only what its source said: the person's recorded answers, or the screens it was read from. The save refuses any other seed. The save is the one script step that writes the model's index, the profile and the decision records.

changes.old: - A named capability the model lacks starts with questions. The run asks for all of them at once, before it opens any change. With no answer, or a domain the model lacks, it stops and says what it needs, and it leaves nothing behind. Inside the loop, that capability becomes the loop's question and the others go on.
changes.new: - A named capability the model lacks starts with questions. The run asks for all of them at once, before it opens any change. With no answer, or a domain the model lacks, it stops and says what it needs, and it leaves nothing behind. Inside the loop, that capability becomes the loop's question and the others go on. The loop is the discovery loop, which reads a prototype once and runs Specify intents, Specify domains and this feature on that reading, in rounds.

changes.old: - A capability from the screens with no known domain waits in a holding folder. It is kept, and it is not ready until it is linked to a domain.
changes.new: - A capability from the screens with no known domain waits in a holding folder. The holding folder is a place in the model for capabilities whose domain is not known yet. It is kept, and it is not ready until it is linked to a domain.

changes.old: - The first run firms a still-rough profile to set, with no decision record. On a set profile, a need above its level stops at the checkpoint as its own line, and each move gets its own decision record. Inside the loop, these records read proposed.
changes.new: - The first run firms a still-rough profile to set, with no decision record. Set means its levels are now committed. The reason there is no record: a rough profile has no committed level yet, so firming it moves nothing. On a set profile, a need above its level stops at the checkpoint as its own line, and each move gets its own decision record. The checkpoint is the one point where the run shows the person every change and, run by hand, waits for a yes before anything is committed. Inside the loop, these records read proposed.

changes.old: - One run has one save, one checkpoint and one commit for all its capabilities. If one cannot pass its checks, the whole run stops and nothing is committed.
changes.new: - One run has one save, one checkpoint and one commit for all its capabilities. The reason: one capability at a time was too slow, and the person approves every capability and every profile move together, before anything is committed. If one cannot pass its checks, the whole run stops and nothing is committed.

changes.old: A person gives a project folder. The run treats it as two Sources: the project's written docs and its running app. It keeps the docs first. It then starts the app the way the README (the project's main instruction file) says, captures the running app the way it captures a deployed site, and stops the app. The intent draft reads both Sources together.
changes.new: A person gives a project folder. The run treats it as two Sources: the project's written docs and its running app. It keeps the docs first. It then starts the app the way the README (the project's main instruction file) says, captures the running app the way it captures a deployed site, and stops the app. The intent draft reads both Sources together. A Source is a saved copy of what a person gave, which later steps read instead of the original. A folder gives two because a runnable source is also run through, so what it does is seen, not only what its docs say. The intent draft is the first version of the business intents, which the person then confirms or drops.

changes.new: - Out: the docs Source: a copy of each written doc at the top of the folder. Its capture record reads "prototype — project". A capture record is what each capture writes about its Source: its kind, the date it was read, who gave it and its saved files.

changes.new: - The agent running the work starts and stops the app by following the README. No fixed script does this, and no check confirms that the app stopped. So an app left running after the capture is not caught.

changes.new: A person gives a document, such as a brief or a PDF. The run saves an exact copy under the document's own name, with the run's evidence, so the document outlives the original file. The run's evidence is the folder where a run keeps what it read and did, committed with its change. At this step the run does not open or read the document. A later step reads the copy and writes what it shows in a separate record beside the copy.

changes.old: - Any file whose name does not end in .html or .htm counts as a document. A video counts too, so today a video is only copied. Reading one belongs to Specify from a video (fn-specify-from-video), and it is not built.
changes.new: - Any file whose name does not end in .html or .htm counts as a document. The reason: a web-page file is a prototype, and Specify from a file (fn-specify-from-file) captures it view by view in a browser. A video counts too, so today a video is only copied. Reading one belongs to Specify from a video (fn-specify-from-video), and it is not built.

changes.old: - The capture does not open the file. So a damaged file, or a format no later step can read, passes this step.
changes.new: - The capture does not open the file. The reason: this step only keeps and records, and saying what a document shows is judgment that a later step does. So a damaged file, or a format no later step can read, passes this step.

changes.old: - The capture record holds the fingerprint of the saved copy. No step works out the original's fingerprint or compares the two.
changes.new: - The capture record holds the fingerprint of the saved copy. A fingerprint is a short code worked out from a file's bytes, so any change to the file changes the code. No step works out the original's fingerprint or compares the two. So the run cannot tell when the copy differs from the original.

changes.old: - Given a brief in a file, when it is captured, then the fingerprint of the copy equals one worked out from the original and the record reads "document".
changes.new: - Given a brief in a file, when it is captured, then the record reads "document" and holds the copy's fingerprint, which equals one the test works out from the original.
